Total revenue across the four stores grew by more than 15%
Riverside grew faster in percentage terms than Hilltop
Harbour's revenue grew by more than $0.5m
solution: Growth: Harbour 0.4 ÷ 4.2 ≈ 9.5%, Hilltop 0.4 ÷ 3.1 ≈ 12.9%, Riverside 0.2 ÷ 5.0 = 4%, Market Square 0.5 ÷ 2.4 ≈ 20.8%

context.text: A transport survey asked 1,000 adults about the vehicles they own. 62% own a car, 38% own a bike, and 15% own both.

More than half of the respondents own neither a car nor a bike
One in five respondents owns both a car and a bike
47% of the respondents own a car but no bike
solution: Car but no bike: 62% − 15% = 47%
Own at least one: 62% + 38% − 15% = 85%, so 15% own neither
Both: 15%, not one in five (20%)
shortcut: Draw two overlapping circles: car only 47, both 15, bike only 23, neither 15.

context.text: A car-sharing club charges members $0.45 per km driven. Each car costs the club $9,000 a year in fixed costs (lease, insurance, parking) plus $0.12 per km in fuel and wear. On average each car is rented out for 18,000 km a year.

prompt: Which statement is supported by these figures?
options: Raising the rate to $0.55 per km would make each car profitable at 18,000 km a year
Each car currently makes a profit
Cutting fixed costs by a quarter would make each car profitable at its current mileage
A car must be rented out for more than 27,000 km a year to break even
solution: Contribution per km: $0.45 − $0.12 = $0.33; at 18,000 km, $5,940 against $9,000 of fixed costs
shortcut: Contribution covers about two thirds of fixed costs (5,940 ÷ 9,000 = 0.66), so mileage must rise by about half: 27,000 km is just short.

context.text: A metal-fabrication firm tracks the prices of its three inputs as indices (2020 = 100). In 2020 steel made up 40% of its input costs, energy 15% and labour 45%. The quantities of each input it uses have not changed.

Steel costs rose by more in percentage terms than energy costs
Labour still makes up more than 45% of input costs in 2024
Energy makes up more than 18% of input costs in 2024
solution: Total rise: about 33%
shortcut: Rebase everything to 100 of 2020 cost; energy grew fastest, so its share must rise from 15% (to above 18%).

2030: Premium 20 < Budget 25; Standard 36 ÷ 81 ≈ 44%

context.text: The manager of a water-treatment plant gives the following facts about its control room.

items: Safety rules require at least two engineers on duty in the control room at all times, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week
The plant employs 8 control-room engineers, each contracted for 40 hours a week, and no one else may staff the control room
Total weekly pay for contracted hours is $14,400, with every engineer on the same hourly rate

Each contracted engineer-hour costs more than $50
Eight engineers working only their contracted hours can provide the minimum cover
At least one engineer must work more than 40 hours in a week
solution: Minimum cover: 2 × 24 × 7 = 336 engineer-hours a week
Contracted hours: 8 × 40 = 320, which is 16 short, so someone must work beyond 40 hours

context.text: A consumer-electronics brand cut the price of its wireless speaker by 20%. Unit sales then rose by 30%, and revenue reached $10.4m.

prompt: Which statement is supported by these figures?
options: Revenue before the price cut was $10m
If each speaker cost half the old price to make, profit rose after the cut
Unit sales needed to rise by only 20% to keep revenue unchanged
The price cut raised revenue by 10%
solution: Revenue factor: 0.8 × 1.3 = 1.04, so revenue before was $10.4m ÷ 1.04 = $10m, a rise of 4%
With unit cost at half the old price: profit before $10m − $5m = $5m; after $10.4m − 1.3 × $5m = $3.9m
Keeping revenue flat after a 20% cut needs 1 ÷ 0.8 = 1.25, a 25% rise in units
shortcut: Price × volume: 0.8 × 1.3 = 1.04. Undoing a 20% cut needs 25% more volume, not 20%.

context.text: A harbour ferry carries 1.46 million passenger trips a year and runs every day of the year. 30% of all trips are made by commuters, who travel only on the 250 working days and make two trips (out and back) on each of those days.

prompt: Which statement can be concluded from these facts?
options: The ferry carries an average of 4,000 passenger trips a day
More than 1,000 different commuters use the ferry on a typical working day
Commuters make more than a third of all trips
Non-commuter trips average more than 3,000 a day
solution: Average trips a day: 1,460,000 ÷ 365 = 4,000
Commuter trips: 30% × 1,460,000 = 438,000, or 1,752 per working day, which is 876 commuters
Non-commuter trips: 1,022,000 ÷ 365 = 2,800 a day; commuters make 30%, less than a third

context.text: The finance director of a large general hospital is preparing a review of non-staff spending, that is, everything the hospital buys other than staff time. She sorts it into three groups.

items: Estate: the hospital's buildings, their rent, repairs and upkeep
Clinical: everything used to diagnose and treat patients
Support: the services that keep the wards and offices running

context.title: Exhibit 1: Non-staff spending, last year

prompt: Which of the following statements can be concluded from the data in Exhibit 1?
options: 52% of all non-staff spending is clinical
28% of all support spending goes on IT services
More than 10% of non-staff spending goes on medical equipment
More than 30% of non-staff spending goes on medicines
solution: Support spending is the last three bars: 6 + 7 + 5 = $18m; IT services: 5 ÷ 18 ≈ 28% of it (true)
Clinical spending is bars 2 to 5: 10 + 31 + 14 + 13 = $68m, which is 61% of $111m, not 52%

Medicines: 31 ÷ 111 ≈ 27.9%, less than 30%

context.text: A regional water company has to report to its regulator where the water it puts into supply ends up. Its planners divide the daily volume into three uses.

items: Network losses: water lost from the company's own pipes before it reaches a customer
Business use: water supplied to any customer that is not a private home
Household use: water supplied to private homes

context.title: Exhibit 1: Water put into supply, average week

prompt: Based on Exhibit 1, which of the following statements is true?
options: 28% of all household use is by apartments
More than 10% of the water put into supply goes to factories
18% of the water put into supply goes to business use
More than an eighth of the water put into supply goes to offices and shops
solution: Household use is the last three bars: 1.1 + 2.0 + 0.8 = 3.9 billion litres a week; apartments: 1.1 ÷ 3.9 ≈ 28% of it (true)
Business use is bars 2 to 5: 0.6 + 0.8 + 0.2 + 0.3 = 1.9 billion litres a week, which is 26% of 7.3 billion litres, not 18%
Factories: 0.6 ÷ 7.3 ≈ 8.2%, less than 10%
Offices and shops: 0.8 ÷ 7.3 ≈ 11.0%, less than an eighth (12.5%)

context.text: The environment team of a city council is drawing up the city's first carbon budget. It puts the city's greenhouse gas emissions into three sectors.

items: Industry: emissions from factories and other industrial sites
Buildings: emissions from heating, cooling and powering any building that is not industrial
Transport: emissions from vehicles on the city's roads

context.title: Exhibit 1: Greenhouse gas emissions by source, last year

prompt: Which of the following statements is a valid conclusion, based on the data presented in Exhibit 1?
options: More than 30% of the city's emissions come from homes
More than 5% of the city's emissions come from public buildings
66% of all transport emissions come from cars
43% of the city's emissions come from buildings
solution: Transport is the last three bars: 4.1 + 0.4 + 1.7 = 6.2 million tonnes; cars: 4.1 ÷ 6.2 ≈ 66% of it (true)
Buildings is bars 2 to 5: 0.9 + 5.4 + 1.8 + 1.2 = 9.3 million tonnes, which is 47% of 19.7 million tonnes, not 43%
Public buildings: 0.9 ÷ 19.7 ≈ 4.6%, less than 5%
Homes: 5.4 ÷ 19.7 ≈ 27.4%, less than 30%

context.text: The research office of a university is reviewing where its research income comes from before a funding round. It sorts every grant and contract into three kinds of funder.

items: Industry: companies paying for research they commission
Public funding: money from any government ministry or agency, at home or abroad
Charities and gifts: money from charities, foundations and private donors

The health ministry: 10 ÷ 153 ≈ 6.5%, less than 7%
Research councils: 58 ÷ 153 ≈ 37.9%, less than 40%

context.text: The strategy team of a national supermarket chain is looking at last year's sales before it sets new space plans for the stores. It puts every product line into one of three categories.

Grocery: all other food and drink
Non-food: everything else the stores sell

36% of all non-food sales are clothing
More than 10% of the chain's sales are household goods
More than a quarter of the chain's sales are tins and dry goods
solution: Grocery is bars 2 to 5: 1.8 + 2.2 + 1.5 + 0.7 = $6.2bn, which is 63% of $9.8bn (true)
Non-food is the last three bars: 0.9 + 0.4 + 0.7 = $2.0bn; clothing: 0.4 ÷ 2.0 = 20% of it, not 36%
Household goods: 0.9 ÷ 9.8 ≈ 9.2%, less than 10%
Tins and dry goods: 2.2 ÷ 9.8 ≈ 22.4%, less than a quarter
shortcut: 10% of $9.8bn is about $1bn and a quarter about $2.5bn, above household goods' $0.9bn and tins' $2.2bn; grocery's $6.2bn is a little under two thirds of $9.8bn.

context.text: The investor relations team of a hotel group is drafting the annual results. The group reports its revenue under three headings.

Food and drink: every meal and drink sold, wherever in the hotel it is served
Other services: anything else that guests and visitors pay for

More than 10% of the group's revenue comes from restaurants
23% of all other services revenue comes from the spa
More than 4% of the group's revenue comes from meeting rooms

Drama: 128 ÷ 549 ≈ 23.3%, less than a quarter

context.text: The board of a regional airline wants a breakdown of last year's operating costs before it renews the leases on its aircraft. The costs fall into three groups.

items: Fuel: the jet fuel burned by the fleet
Fleet and airports: all other costs of flying the aircraft, apart from staff
Staff: pay and benefits of the airline's own employees

More than 5% of operating costs are carbon permits

solution: Aircraft leasing: 154 ÷ 908 ≈ 17.0% of operating costs, more than 15% (true)

Carbon permits: 37 ÷ 908 ≈ 4.1%, less than 5%

context.text: A paint manufacturer wants to know what has been behind sales growth in its ten product lines over the last 10 years: higher Price or more Volume (litres sold). Exhibit 2 shows, for each line, average annual sales growth and how much of that growth came from Price and how much from Volume, as percentages adding up to 100%.

context.title: Exhibit 2: Sales growth by product line, split into Price and Volume, last 10 years
context.note: Number after each bar: the line's average yearly sales growth, %

prompt: Which of the following statements is TRUE, based on the information provided in Exhibit 2?
options: Volume grew by 27% across all ten product lines over the last 10 years
Exterior paint had the greatest growth in Price over the last 10 years
Sealants had the least growth in Price over the last 10 years
Spray paint had the least growth in Volume over the last 10 years
solution: Each source's growth = total growth × its share.
Price: Exterior paint 5.1 × 109.3% = 5.6, the highest (next are Interior paint 4.6 and Primers 3.5), so B is true.
Least Price growth is Adhesives (1.6 × 29.3% = 0.5), not Sealants (0.7).
Least Volume growth is Exterior paint (5.1 × −9.3% = −0.47), not Spray paint (−0.24).
Nothing supports a 27% figure for Volume.
shortcut: Only a line with both a big total and a big Price share can lead: Exterior paint grew fastest of all, and its Price share is over 100%.

context.text: A hotel group is looking at revenue growth at its ten hotels over the last 8 years. Revenue rises when the average Room rate goes up or when Occupancy, the share of rooms sold each night, improves. Exhibit 3 gives each hotel's average annual revenue growth, split into the part due to Room rate and the part due to Occupancy, each as a percentage of that growth (together 100%).

context.title: Exhibit 3: Revenue growth per hotel and its drivers, last 8 years
context.note: Figure at the end of each bar: average annual revenue growth, %

prompt: Based on Exhibit 3, which of the following statements is TRUE?
options: Occupancy grew by 30% across all ten hotels over the last 8 years
Lakeside had the greatest growth in Occupancy over the last 8 years
Station had the least growth in Room rate over the last 8 years
Airport had the least growth in Occupancy over the last 8 years
solution: A driver's growth is the hotel's total growth multiplied by that driver's share.
Room rate: Station 1.2 × 33.8% = 0.41, the lowest (next are Lakeside 0.52 and University 0.69), so C is true.
Greatest Occupancy growth is Riverside (5.8 × 50.9% = 3.0), not Lakeside (2.7).
Least Occupancy growth is Marina (4.6 × −12.5% = −0.58), not Airport (−0.28).
Nothing supports a 30% figure for Occupancy.
shortcut: Only a hotel with a small total and a small Room rate share can be lowest: Station's 1.2 × about a third = 0.4, below Lakeside's 3.2 × 16% = 0.5.

context.text: A cinema chain has split the growth in box-office revenue at each of its ten cinemas over the last 6 years into two parts: Admissions (tickets sold) and Ticket price (the average paid per ticket). Exhibit 2 sets out each cinema's average annual box-office growth, with the percentage of it explained by each part; for every cinema the two percentages make 100%.

context.title: Exhibit 2: Box-office growth by cinema and its two parts, last 6 years
context.note: Value next to each bar: average annual box-office growth, %

prompt: Which of the following statements is TRUE, based on the data above?
options: Admissions grew by 25% across all ten cinemas over the last 6 years
Cinema 1 had the greatest growth in Ticket price over the last 6 years
Cinema 10 had the least growth in Ticket price over the last 6 years
Cinema 2 had the least growth in Admissions over the last 6 years
solution: Multiply each cinema's total growth by a part's share to get that part's growth.
Admissions: Cinema 2 4.9 × −8.2% = −0.40, the lowest (next are Cinema 1 −0.28 and Cinema 3 −0.12), so D is true.
Greatest Ticket price growth is Cinema 4 (6.2 × 91.4% = 5.7), not Cinema 1 (1.4).
Least Ticket price growth is Cinema 8 (1.4 × 44.8% = 0.6), not Cinema 10 (1.0).
Nothing supports a 25% figure for Admissions.
shortcut: Only the three cinemas with a negative Admissions share can be lowest: Cinema 2's 4.9 × −8% is about −0.4, below Cinema 1's 1.1 × −25% (about −0.28).

context.text: Our client franchises a burger brand across the ten regions of its home country. Over the last 9 years, regional sales have grown either through new Outlets (more restaurants open) or through higher Sales per outlet. Exhibit 4 gives, region by region, average annual sales growth and what percentage of it came from Outlets and from Sales per outlet (together 100%).

context.title: Exhibit 4: Sales growth by region and its sources, last 9 years
context.note: Figure beside each bar: average annual sales growth, %

prompt: Which of the following statements is TRUE based on the information provided in Exhibit 4?
options: Sales per outlet grew by 31% across all ten regions over the last 9 years
South-West had the greatest growth in Sales per outlet over the last 9 years
South had the least growth in Outlets over the last 9 years
Capital had the least growth in Sales per outlet over the last 9 years
solution: Growth from Outlets or from Sales per outlet = total growth × its share.
Outlets: South 1.0 × 36.9% = 0.37, the lowest (next are South-West 0.50 and North-West 0.77), so C is true.
Greatest Sales per outlet growth is East (5.9 × 54.7% = 3.2), not South-West (2.9).
Least Sales per outlet growth is Central (4.4 × −14.9% = −0.66), not Capital (−0.33).

shortcut: South has the smallest total growth of any region and only about a third of it from Outlets; the two regions with smaller Outlets shares grew about three times as fast.

context.text: A dairy cooperative has looked at what lay behind the increase in milk output at its 10 largest member farms over the last 7 years. A farm produces more milk through better Yield (milk per cow) or a bigger Herd size (cows milked).
